indiaMissions/india-azariah-indigenous/t: V. S. Azariah, the Indian Missionary Society and the National Missionary Society
indiaMissions/india-azariah-indigenous/s: At the start of the twentieth century Indian Christians began founding their own missions. The Indian Missionary Society of Tinnevelly (1903) and the National Missionary Society (1905), both inspired by the young YMCA secretary V. S. Azariah, sent Indian missionaries with Indian money under Indian leadership. Azariah himself went as an IMS missionary to Dornakal and in 1912 became the first Indian bishop of the Anglican Church in India, presiding over a mass movement of Dalits and low-caste Telugus that brought roughly 200,000 people into the church and helping to create the Church of South India.

By 1900 Indian Christians had been criticising missionary control for decades. Independent bodies such as the Hindu Church of Lord Jesus (Tirunelveli, 1858), the National Church of India (Madras, 1886) and Kali Charan Banerji's Christo Samaj in Calcutta (1887) had tried to break free, and the Mar Thoma Syrian Church's Evangelistic Association (1888) and Maramon Convention (1895) showed the energy of Kerala's Syrian Christians. The decisive initiative came from a young Tamil Anglican of the Nadar community, Vedanayagam Samuel Azariah, born in 1874 at Vellalanvilai in Tirunelveli district, the son of a village priest. Educated at CMS schools and Madras Christian College, he became a travelling secretary of the YMCA from 1895, working with the American student leaders Sherwood Eddy and John R. Mott.

On 12 February 1903 Azariah and fellow Tirunelveli Christians founded the Indian Missionary Society of Tinnevelly at Palayamkottai, the first Protestant missionary society in India run entirely by Indians. Its chosen field was Dornakal, in the Telugu-speaking territories of the Nizam of Hyderabad, and its first missionaries went there in the following years. On Christmas Day 1905, in William Carey's library at Serampore, Azariah and leaders from across India founded the National Missionary Society with the motto ‘Indian men, Indian money and Indian leadership’. The NMS, interdenominational in scope, opened fields in the Punjab (Montgomery district), North Arcot and later other regions, and its general secretary K. T. Paul became one of the most respected Indian Christian public figures.

At the World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh in 1910 Azariah, one of the very few Asian delegates, gave the speech that made him famous: missionaries had given their goods and their lives for India, he said, but they had withheld friendship — ‘You have given your goods to feed the poor. You have given your bodies to be burned. We also ask for love. Give us friends!’ He had by then left the YMCA, been ordained (1909) and gone to Dornakal himself as an IMS missionary. On 29 December 1912 he was consecrated bishop of the new diocese of Dornakal in St Paul's Cathedral, Calcutta — the first Indian bishop of the Anglican Church in India — despite opposition from missionaries who doubted that an Indian could lead Europeans.

Dornakal became the scene of one of the largest Christian mass movements in India. Malas and Madigas, the main Dalit communities of the Telugu country, joined the church village by village; from the 1920s growing numbers of Sudra caste peasants followed. Azariah insisted that converts be well taught before baptism, that each village congregation support its own teacher-catechist, that every baptised Christian lay hands on his or her own head and say ‘Woe is me if I preach not the gospel’, and that Indian customs be adopted in worship. The Cathedral of the Epiphany at Dornakal, built over more than two decades, mixed Hindu and Islamic architectural motifs. His wife Anbu Mariammal led work among women. By his death on 1 January 1945, the movements he inspired had brought roughly 200,000 people into the church.

Azariah also chaired the National Christian Council and was a principal architect of the negotiations that produced the Church of South India in 1947, uniting Anglicans with Methodists, Presbyterians and Congregationalists. His advocacy of mass conversion brought him into conflict with M. K. Gandhi, who in the 1930s denounced conversions of the ‘untouchables’ as a spiritual and political threat, especially after B. R. Ambedkar's 1935 announcement that he would leave Hinduism; Gandhi is reported to have called Azariah his ‘enemy number one’. Azariah, for his part, opposed separate electorates for Christians and supported Indian self-rule while maintaining a close relationship with the British church.

The IMS and NMS survive as Indian mission agencies, and Azariah's principles — indigenous leadership, self-support, lay evangelism and church union — became the common sense of Indian Protestantism after independence. Critics have noted that the Dornakal movement left caste distinctions intact within congregations, with Mala, Madiga and Sudra Christians often worshipping separately, and that Azariah's moderate politics made him suspect to nationalists. His life nonetheless marked the moment when Indian Christians took charge of mission in their own country.

indiaMissions/india-azariah-indigenous/l: Azariah, the Indian Missionary Society and the National Missionary Society mark the point at which Indian Christians took over mission in India. Azariah's appeal for friendship at Edinburgh, his leadership of a mass movement and his work for church union shaped Indian Protestantism, while his conflict with Gandhi anticipated the later national argument over conversion. The caste divisions that persisted in the Dornakal church show how far indigenous leadership could go in changing village society, and where it stopped.

indiaMissions/india-pentecostals/title: Indian Pentecostalism (Mukti, IPC, Ceylon Pentecostal Mission, Assemblies of God)
indiaMissions/india-pentecostals/place/n: Kumbanad, Kerala (headquarters of the Indian Pentecostal Church of God)
indiaMissions/india-pentecostals/summary: Indian Pentecostalism grew from the Mukti revival of 1905 and the arrival of Azusa Street missionaries in 1906–07, but took root above all through Indian leaders in Kerala and Tamil Nadu: K. E. Abraham's Indian Pentecostal Church of God, Pastor Paul's Ceylon Pentecostal Mission (The Pentecostal Mission), the Assemblies of God and the Church of God. Spreading among Syrian Christians, Dalits and later in the north, Pentecostal and charismatic churches are now the fastest-growing part of Indian Christianity, with millions of adherents, many in independent churches the census does not count separately.
indiaMissions/india-pentecostals/story:
South India had seen revivals with ecstatic features long before Azusa Street. In 1860 the Tamil evangelist John Christian Aroolappen, a disciple of the Brethren pioneer Anthony Norris Groves, reported prophecy and speaking in tongues in Tirunelveli, and the revival spread to Travancore; Kerala experienced further revivals in the 1870s, including the millenarian ‘Six Years' Party’ of Justus Joseph. In 1905 the revival at Pandita Ramabai's Mukti Mission near Pune, and by late 1906 its reports of tongues, made India one of the original centres of the twentieth-century Pentecostal movement. Minnie Abrams' account of Mukti was read in America and Chile.

Azusa Street sent Alfred G. Garr and his wife Lillian, who arrived in Calcutta at the end of 1906 and held meetings at the Bow Bazar Baptist chapel early in 1907. Garr had expected that tongues would give missionaries foreign languages for preaching; when this proved not to be so, he and others reinterpreted tongues as prayer language, a turning point in Pentecostal theology. Max Wood Moorhead in Bombay published reports of Pentecost in India, Thomas Ball Barratt visited in 1908, and George Berg brought the message to Travancore in 1909. The most important foreign worker in Kerala was Robert F. Cook, an American who arrived in 1913 and from 1914 worked from Mulakuzha; his mission affiliated with the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) in 1936. American Assemblies of God missionaries worked in Travancore from the 1920s and in the north from the 1910s.

Indian leaders soon led the movement. K. E. Abraham, a Syrian Christian schoolteacher, worked with Cook in the 1920s but in 1930 led most Indian believers out of the foreign-funded mission to build a self-supporting church; the Indian Pentecostal Church of God, which traces its beginnings to 1924, was registered in 1935 and made its headquarters at Kumbanad. Splits produced further bodies, notably the Sharon Fellowship Church under P. J. Thomas in 1953. Pastor Paul, a Hindu convert from Kerala, founded the Ceylon Pentecostal Mission in Colombo in 1923 with Alwin R. de Alwis; known in India as The Pentecostal Mission, it became famous for its celibate ministers dressed in white, communal ‘faith homes’, refusal of medicine and strict separation from the world, and spread through Tamil Nadu and Kerala with its headquarters later in Chennai.

Pentecostalism in Kerala drew converts from the Syrian Christian and Anglican (CSI) churches, which accused it of ‘sheep-stealing’, and from Dalit communities attracted by healing, exorcism and a message of equality before the Spirit. Caste nevertheless reproduced itself: Syrian Christian families largely controlled leadership, Dalit Pentecostals complained of segregated seating, separate burial and exclusion from office, and some churches divided along caste lines, such as the Church of God in Kerala, which split in 1972 into a largely Syrian ‘Kerala Division’ and a largely Dalit ‘Kerala State’ church. Kerala Pentecostals in turn became major missionaries to North India and the Gulf.

From the 1970s healing evangelists and charismatic movements spread the Pentecostal style far beyond Kerala. D. G. S. Dhinakaran's ‘Jesus Calls’ ministry (from 1970s Chennai) reached millions by prayer towers, radio and television; independent churches multiplied in Hyderabad, Bangalore, Mumbai and Delhi; and from the 2000s Pentecostal ‘ministries’ grew rapidly among Dalit and other poor communities in Punjab, often led by charismatic healers. Catholic charismatic renewal, especially the Divine Retreat Centre at Muringoor (Kerala), mirrored the same spirituality. Some of these movements attracted scandal: the Punjab pastor Bajinder Singh was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2025 for rape, and others have faced charges of fraudulent healing and financial abuse.

Pentecostals are now often at the centre of controversies over conversion. Hindu nationalist groups accuse them of aggressive proselytism, inducement by promises of healing and denigration of Hindu deities, and they have been disproportionately targeted in violence and in prosecutions under state anti-conversion laws. Their growth has made Indian Christianity more lay-led, more independent and more working-class, and has shifted its centre of energy from the historic denominations towards thousands of small congregations, many of which the census and most church statistics do not separately record.

indiaMissions/india-pentecostals/legacy: Indian Pentecostalism shows the indigenous energy of Indian Christianity. It began in an Indian women's revival at Mukti, was soon led by Indians and spread mainly through ordinary believers. It has given Dalits and the poor a religion of healing, dignity and lay leadership, while repeating the caste divisions of the older churches and producing schisms and scandals. Pentecostals are now the most visible Christians in many parts of India and are at the centre of the national dispute over conversion.
